newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM denies role in Cambodia logging row.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM denies role in Cambodia logging row.

text.p: Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh on Monday denied allegations by politicians that he and his family had taken bribes to allow businessmen to haul logs from Cambodia into Thailand.
"The documents clearly show who were involved and who were not," Chavalit told reporters and assigned the government spokesman to clarify the issue on his behalf from a 32-page document.
In his clarification, Chavalit said only the interior ministry was authorised to permit Thai firms to haul logs from Cambodia into the country.
As he had been defence minister in the previous Thai government of prime minister Banharn Silpa-archa, he had no authority to allow anyone to haul Cambodian logs, he added.
The London-based environment group Global Witness has accused the Thai government of taking bribes to allow the hauling of Cambodian logs.

Recently, the Cambodian government accused Thai businessmen of violating its order banning logging from April 31, 1996. The government charged that fresh-cut logs were still finding their way into Thailand until the end of 1996.

Government spokesman Varathep Rattankorn told reporters that Chavalit had met Cambodian Agriculture Minister Tao Seng Huo early last year to clarify that he was not responsible for licensing Thai logging firms to do business in Cambodia.

Information in the document released by Chavalit indicated that ex-prime minister Banharn, in his role as minister of interior last year, had permitted 12 Thai companies to haul logs and process wood from Cambodia using temporary passes.
"I have no intention to put the blame on anyone but merely want the public to see who was involved and who was not," Chavalit said, apparently referring to Banharn's role.
Banharn told reporters last week that he only signed documents to allow companies who had legally acquired logs from Cambodia to undertake the business.
